# Actual one-ear cap/section formulas and a symmetric quadrilateral certificate

This note retains actual polygon geometry. It proves the proposed generalized Lorentz inequalities for a specific family of reflection-symmetric quadrilaterals. It does not prove them for arbitrary quadrilaterals or arbitrary convex bodies, and it does not assert mixed-fiber compatibility.

## 1. Exact formulas for one added ear

Let T have three strict unique-signature vertices P_1,P_2,P_3 for the canonical normals `(1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)`, with zero interior. Add a fourth point Q in the double-signature sector Y_1, across the edge P_2 P_3, and assume the resulting convex quadrilateral has cyclic vertices P_1,P_2,Q,P_3. Its added ear is the triangle P_2 Q P_3; denote its area by E>0.

For cap 2 put

    p=v_2.P_2>0, w=-v_2.P_3>0, v=v_2.Q>0.

The ear's negative-side portion is the triangle at P_3. Its fraction is

    w^2/[(w+p)(w+v)].

Therefore the added raw cap area and the added coarea chord are exactly

    Delta Q_2=E[1-w^2/((w+p)(w+v))],
    Delta sigma_2=2Ew/[(w+p)(w+v)].                      (1)

The sections of T and of the ear meet only at their common edge-crossing point, so their coarea lengths add. The old cap is the vertex triangle at P_2 and has `2Q_2^old=p sigma_2^old`. Thus its virtual height changes by

    2Q_2^new/sigma_2^new
       =p+[Delta sigma_2/(sigma_2^old+Delta sigma_2)]
                                      v(1+p/w).         (2)

The same formulas hold for cap 3 after interchanging the two other unique vertices. Cap 1 and its chord are unchanged, because the whole ear is strictly on its negative side. Importantly, the ear need not lie wholly in Y_1: near P_2 and P_3 it also occupies their unique sectors. Formula (1) retains this mass exactly.

## 2. A complete symmetric family

Take arbitrary x,u,v>0 and delta>=0, and set

    P_1=(2v,-v), P_2=(-x,x+u), P_3=(-x,-u),
    Q=(-x-delta,(x+delta)/2).

For delta>0 these are cyclic vertices P_1,P_2,Q,P_3 of a convex quadrilateral. Indeed the determinant-one shear `(X,Y)->(X,Y+X/2)` sends them to

    (2v,0), (-x,x/2+u), (-x-delta,0), (-x,-x/2-u),

whose two diagonal segments cross in their relative interiors. At delta=0 Q lies on P_2 P_3 and the body is the original triangle. Zero is interior in every case. The reflection `(X,Y)->(X,-X-Y)` fixes the source and interchanges caps 2 and 3.

Put L=x+2v. The total area, cap 1 data, and the common cap 2/3 data are

    k=(L+delta)(x+2u)/2,
    sigma_1=2v(x+2u)/L,
    Q_1=v sigma_1,

    sigma=sigma_2=sigma_3
      =(x+2u)[v/(x+u+v)+(x+delta)/(x+delta+2u)],

    Q_c=Q_2=Q_3
      =L(x+u)^2/[2(x+u+v)]
         +delta(x+2u)/2-delta u^2/(x+delta+2u).           (3)

The total and cap 1 formulas are triangle areas. The common cap and chord formulas follow either by the two exact intercepts on `Y=0` or from (1). Define

    H_2=2Q_c/sigma, H=v+H_2,
    f_i=2 sqrt(k Q_i)/(sigma_i H).                       (4)

Equivalently these are `f_i=2a_i/sqrt(q_i)`, where `q_i=Q_i/k` and `a_i=(q_i/sigma_i)/sum_j(q_j/sigma_j)`. Thus these are exactly the quantities appearing in the generalized ordinary Lorentz question. We have f_2=f_3.

**Theorem.** Every body in this family satisfies

    f_i+(f_j+f_l)^2/4<=2                               (5)

for all three indices. If delta>0 all three inequalities are strict.

## 3. Exact positive deficit certificate

Define the positive polynomial

    D=delta u+2delta v+delta x+2uv+ux+2vx+x^2.

Substitution of (3) gives

    H_2=[delta^2 u+delta^2 v+delta^2 x+delta u^2
          +2delta uv+3delta ux+3delta vx+2delta x^2
          +2u^2v+u^2x+4uvx+2ux^2+2vx^2+x^3]/D.          (6)

Furthermore the following rational identity holds:

    2H^2-(L+delta/2)H-2k H_2/sigma
      =delta(delta+2v+x)(u+v+x) P/(2D^2),                (7)

where every coefficient of P is positive:

    P=delta^2 u+delta^2 x+delta u^2+3delta ux
        +2delta x^2+2u^2v+u^2x+2ux^2+x^3.

These identities follow by multiplying through the displayed positive denominators in (3); expansion and collecting equal powers of delta gives the displayed polynomials. Hence (7) is nonnegative, and strictly positive for delta>0.

Directly from (3)–(4),

    f_1=sqrt(L(L+delta))/H,
    f_2^2=2k H_2/(sigma H^2).

Arithmetic-geometric mean gives `sqrt(L(L+delta))<=L+delta/2`. Together with (7), this proves `f_1+f_2^2<=2`, with strictness when delta>0. This is (5) for index 1.

To obtain the other two inequalities, write r=f_1 and s=f_2=f_3. We have `r+s^2<=2`, so 0<s<sqrt(2) and r<=2-s^2. Consequently

    s+(r+s)^2/4 <= s+(2-s^2+s)^2/4 <=2,

because the exact last deficit is

    4[2-s-(2-s^2+s)^2/4]=(4-s^2)(s-1)^2>=0.

For delta>0 the first comparison is strict since r<2-s^2 and r+s>0. This proves the full theorem for the actual quadrilateral family. The asymmetric one-ear case is not covered by the positive polynomial (7).
